extracted.intended_audience: literate British public and policymakers concerned with the French Revolution and constitutional design (late 18th century)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts normative criteria and cautions for designing/evaluating constitutions, executive authority, and monetary policy as argued in a political pamphlet critiquing the French Revolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paper circulation and confiscation
rubrics_metrics.description: The mixing of confiscated land into a paper currency (assignats) volatilizes landed property and creates uncertainty in its value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke warns that continually drawing out confiscated land for sale and mixing it into paper circulation 'incorporates' the spirit of money-jobbing and speculation into land itself, making that species of property 'volatilized' and subject to 'an unnatural and monstrous activity' which places control in the hands of managers and speculators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Speculation as a national policy (avoid making a nation of gamesters)
rubrics_metrics.description: A political economy organized around speculation and gaming (making 'speculation as extensive as life') corrupts civic life and economic purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text condemns founding a commonwealth upon gaming: turning inhabitants into 'a nation of gamesters' diverts hopes and fears from ordinary channels into impulses of chance, creating an 'epidemic distemper' and making society hemmed by speculation rather than stable productive activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monetary stability essential for labour and economy
rubrics_metrics.description: A currency whose value fluctuates rapidly (e.g., assignats losing value day to day) destroys incentives to labour, save, and make careful provision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke points out practical harms: 'What he receives in the morning will not have the same value at night' and a peasant cannot calculate or rely on pay, so 'industry must wither away' and 'economy must be driven from your country.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid entrusting landed property to mere money-dealers
rubrics_metrics.description: Those habituated to adventuring and money-jobbing will treat land as a commodity to buy and resell rather than to cultivate; agricultural management requires experienced local knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: He contrasts the insight of an old peasant or monk with that of bank directors, arguing 'one old experienced peasant is worth them all' and that usurers are not tutors of agriculture; financiers will 'purchase to job out again' rather than farm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevent concentration of economic and political power in cities (Paris)
rubrics_metrics.description: Constitutions that centralize monetary and legislative control in a single city allow that city and its directors to dominate the whole nation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke asserts that power over monied and landed circulation will 'settle in the towns' and that Paris, 'now become the centre and focus of jobbing,' will command legislative and executive government; other divisions are left weak and disconnected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve natural local/provincial attachments
rubrics_metrics.description: Artificial 'geometrical' divisions and administrative remapping that ignore habitual provincial bonds will fail to create genuine civic attachment and weaken the state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: He argues that people do not become zealous citizens by square measurement—public affections begin in families, neighbourhoods, and provincial connections; breaking old connexions risks destroying the ties that train citizens for larger public concern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislative power must have external checks (need for a senate/council)
rubrics_metrics.description: A republic composed solely of one active legislative assembly without a senatorial council or intermediary body lacks steadiness, consistency, and an appropriate instrument for foreign relations and long-term direction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke insists that 'they have forgot to constitute a senate, or something of that nature' and that such a body provides a middle place between supreme power and the executive, giving bias, steadiness, and consistency to state proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive office must have deliberative discretion and means to reward
rubrics_metrics.description: An executive reduced to a mere machine without discretionary power and without the ability to reward (honours, pensions, lands) cannot command faithful service and will be forced to rely on fear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: He criticizes the degraded king who 'serves only as a notary' and is 'no more the fountain of honour than he is the fountain of justice,' arguing that without the means to reward, 'those who serve the king can be actuated by no natural motive but fear.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Prerogative of peace and war as a key executive trust
rubrics_metrics.description: The right to make peace and war is a dangerous but necessary prerogative to vest in an executive (or accompanied by auxiliary trusts) to prevent foreign powers from personally intriguing with legislators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke suggests that leaving the right of peace and war to the executive (or providing correctives if not left) is one way to keep foreign potentates from 'intriguing distinctly and personally with the members of your Assembly' and fomenting factions directed by foreign powers.

rubrics_metrics.name: A recognized source of justice and dignified judicial function
rubrics_metrics.description: Removing the fountain of justice from the sovereign or degrading the judicial function strips dignity and undermines public confidence in administration of justice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: He laments that the king is not the fountain of justice and that judges are nominated without his proposal or veto; as a result the king becomes 'nothing more than a chief of ... jailers, and hangmen' and justice is made vile and odious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design incentives beyond mere responsibility for ministers
rubrics_metrics.description: Holding ministers 'responsible' is insufficient to produce zealous, effective governance; structural incentives and rewards are required to generate active service rather than fear-driven obedience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke notes that responsibility 'prevents crimes' but 'will never make a nation glorious' and that fear-based service yields poor results; ministers must have motives (honour, reward, interest) to perform zealously.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid constitutional designs that empower an ignoble oligarchy of speculators
rubrics_metrics.description: Institutions that combine directors of assignats, trustees for sale of church lands, attorneys, agents, and money-jobbers produce an ignoble oligarchy that can absorb and destroy older social orders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: He warns that such corporations will compose 'an ignoble oligarchy, founded on the destruction of the crown, the church, the nobility, and the people,' where equality and rights are 'absorbed, sunk, and lost for ever.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitute an executive that can command respect and harmonious obedience
rubrics_metrics.description: If the chief executive is perceived as degraded or without legitimate prerogatives, foreign states and domestic subordinates will treat him with contempt, making coherent governance impossible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke argues a state of contempt is unfit for a prince; a king who is 'degraded' cannot infuse vigour into measures or be relied upon by ministers or foreign powers; better to discard such an impotent office than retain it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid creating an assembly without fundamental laws, maxims, or procedural rules
rubrics_metrics.description: A sovereign assembly endowed with 'every possible power, and no possible external control' and lacking established maxims or respected rules of proceeding will overreach and produce instability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: He describes the National Assembly as a body 'without fundamental laws, without established maxims, without respected rules of proceeding' and warns that its powers are always taken at the utmost stretch of legislative competency, yielding perpetual emergency-style governance.
